These two additional analyses suggest that, regardless of their exact status (which remains challenging to
infer), whether emerging, coding, or relics of pseudogenes whose ancestral origin is no longer detectable,
these potentially overlooked ORFs are few in number and, overall, would not alter the main trends if
included in our analyses. Yet, it should be noted that neither annotation pipelines nor experimental
methods can fully capture the complexity of the ORF repertoire. Notably, Vakirlis et al. identified 28
unannotated ORFs with adaptive potential in yeast through large-scale overexpression screens17. These
thymine-rich ORFs often encode transmembrane domains and show no observable fitness impact upon
disruption, raising questions about their evolutionary fate. The authors interestingly discussed the
possibility that beneficial effects observed under laboratory conditions may not have the same effect in
natural environments, particularly since their screen involved artificially high expression levels. They further
point out that adaptive potential (i) does not guarantee fixation, since some ORFs may be beneficial under
certain conditions but deleterious in others, and (ii) may involve tradeoffs that hinder long-term retention.
Their work underscores the complexity of annotating such ORFs and highlights the possibility that some
relevant and/or adaptive ORFs may escape detection/annotation. It also raises important questions about
the evolutionary fate and genomic status of these potentially overlooked ORFs, especially in light of two
key observations: CDSs across nearly all eukaryotic genomes are significantly more GC-rich than noncoding
regions (Figure S1A), and transmembrane domains remain underrepresented in proteomes20.

on S. cerevisiae, one of the best-annotated genomes, and searched for potential additional coding ORFs that
may have been missed during annotation. We screened yeast iORFs against those of its five neighboring
species, retained those with DIAMONDv281 matches in at least four neighbors, and tested them for
signatures of purifying selection. We identified 23 ORFs under selection, specific to Saccharomyces (Table
S2), and reconstructed their ancestral sequences. Although their GC enrichment was less pronounced than
that of the 227 ancestral ORFs reconstructed based on the S. cerevisiae annotation, these sequences still
differ from iORFs in both GC content and length, remaining longer and GC-richer (Mann-Whitney U test
(one-sided), P = 2.7x10-7 and 2.1x10-2, respectively)(Figure S15). As an additional control, we considered
the study by Wacholder et al.4, who compiled 412 ribosome profiling datasets from S. cerevisiae, producing
the most comprehensive yeast translational landscape to date. Their annotation-independent approach
identified approximately 19,000 translated unannotated ORFs. However, only 14 showed signatures of
selection, nine of which had homologs outside Saccharomyces and were likely ancient4. Among the five
remaining candidates, three were lacking homologs for ancestral reconstruction. Interestingly, the two
reconstructed ancestral sequences are longer (61 and 130 residues) and GC-richer (47% and 42%) than
typical iORFs.
These results suggest that potentially overlooked de novo genes are not numerous and, overall, would not
contradict our conclusions if included in our analyses. Yet, it should be noted that neither annotation
pipelines nor experimental methods can fully capture ORF diversity. Notably, Vakirlis et al. identified 28
unannotated ORFs with adaptive potential in yeast through large-scale overexpression screens41. These
thymine-rich ORFs often encode transmembrane domains and show no fitness impact upon disruption. The
authors interestingly discussed the possibility that beneficial effects observed under laboratory conditions
may not apply in natural environments, and that adaptive potential does not guarantee fixation, as trade-
offs may hinder long-term retention. Their work underscores the complexity of ORF annotation and the
possibility that some adaptive ORFs escape detection, and raises important questions about the evolutionary
fate of these ORFs regarding two key observations: CDSs in nearly all eukaryotes are GC-richer than
noncoding regions (Figure S1A), and transmembrane domains remain underrepresented in proteomes82.”

We apologize for the lack of clarity and statistical analyses supporting the interpretations, and thank the
Reviewer for this helpful feedback. In response, we now provide statistical analyses to support our claims,
which also allowed us to better describe the trends observed in the initial plot. Specifically, we calculated
the log fold change (LFC) of each codon group to quantify its frequency deviation in real CDSs compared to
scrambled ones. These results are now presented in a new panel (Figure 1B – see below), enabling a clearer
classification of codon groups that was more difficult to infer from the qualitative analysis of the initial plot.
In addition, we quantified the variation in codon group frequencies across genomes for iORFs (x-axis) and
CDSs (y-axis). This analysis, now presented by a new panel (Figure 1C – see below), explicitly measures the
extent to which the frequency of a codon group varies across genomes in iORFs and CDSs. Variation was
assessed by the standard deviations (SDs) of each codon group’s frequency distribution, with high SDs
indicating high variability according to GC content, and low SDs indicating more stable frequencies. Codons
near the diagonal vary similarly in CDSs and iORFs, whereas those in the middle-right region of the plot (e.g.,
NTN, NGN) vary widely in iORFs but remain constrained in CDSs (Figure 1C).
Finally, we now report the distribution of codon group frequencies in real and scrambled CDSs across the
3,379 genomes as boxplots (new panel C of Figure S1) and include statistical comparisons in the text where
appropriate. The revised text now reads:
“Figure 1B shows the log fold change (LFC) of each codon group representing the deviation of its frequency
in real CDSs compared to scrambled ones. Figure 1C illustrates the variation in its frequency across genomes
for iORFs (x-axis) and CDSs (y-axis). Variation is quantified by the standard deviation (SD) of a codon group’s
frequency distribution, with high SDs indicating high variability according to GC content, and low SDs
indicating more stable frequencies. Codons near the diagonal vary similarly in CDSs and iORFs, whereas
those in the middle-right region of the plot (e.g., NTN, NGN) vary widely in iORFs but remain constrained in
CDSs (Figure 1C).
Several codon groups exhibit small LFCs, reflecting similar frequencies in real and scrambled CDSs (Figure
1B). Notably, mixed AT/GC codons (e.g., TCN, CAN, or GTN) typically show little variation in both iORFs and
CDSs (bottom-left corner of Figure 1C), reflecting low sensitivity to GC content. Overall, most codons have
absolute LFCs below 0.5, but four groups show stronger deviations (LFCs > 0.75): TAN, TGN, CGN, and GAN.
Their median frequencies differ significantly from those of scrambled CDSs (Mann-Whitney U test, (two-
sided), all P < 1 × 10-16)(Figure S1C). TAN and TGN comprise the three stop codons and the rare amino acids
tryptophan and cysteine, explaining their strong depletion in CDSs relative to expectations (Figure 1B, Figure
S1C). CGN codons, which encode arginine, are also markedly depleted (Figure 1B, Figure S1C). CpG sites,
consisting of cytosine followed by guanine, are prone to methylation and are hypermutable because
methylated cytosines frequently undergo deamination to thymine51. Such mutations can generate TGN
codons, which may introduce deleterious changes and thereby contribute to the observed depletion of CGN
codons. GAN codons, encoding aspartate and glutamate, display the highest LFC, and a low frequency
variation in CDSs (0.116 ± 0.005) across genomes (Figure 1B-C). Previous studies showed that high
proportions of negative charges on protein surfaces prevent promiscuous interactions with the negatively
charged, abundant ribosomes52, and stretches of such residues optimize translation by facilitating the
nascent peptide’s passage through the negatively charged ribosomal exit tunnel53. In yeast, we also found
a correlation between negative charge frequency and protein abundance, suggesting that a higher
frequency of negative charges in abundant proteins may favor their translation efficiency and reduce
nonspecific interactions with ribosomes23. Finally, the NTN group, encoding most hydrophobic residues,
stands out in Figure 1C, showing the widest variation in iORFs but constrained frequencies in CDSs (0.27 ±
0.01). This suggests that selection acts to maintain optimal hydrophobicity for protein folding, preserving
enough hydrophobic residues in GC-rich species for proper folding while reducing their frequency in AT-rich
species to prevent aggregation. This aligns with Dill’s classic theory, which proposed that protein stability
depends on an optimal fraction of hydrophobic residues54.”

We thank the Reviewer for raising this point. We have now introduced a new test to identify breakpoints
within a sequence of values for each species – specifically, the medians of the GAN distribution of each
phylostratum. To do so, we fitted three Bayesian piecewise-linear models (null: no breakpoint, one
breakpoint, and two breakpoints) using the mcp package21. Model performance was evaluated by leave-
one-out cross-validation22, extracting the expected log-predictive density (ELPD) and its standard error.
Pairwise ELPD differences were calculated, and a more complex model (e.g., two breakpoints over one
breakpoint, or one breakpoint over null model) was accepted only when its improvement (DELPD) exceeded
the combined standard error. Posterior mean breakpoints were then extracted from the model estimates
and mapped back onto the corresponding phylostrata for the 19 species in which at least one breakpoint
was detected.
This analysis allowed us to pinpoint breakpoints across GAN phylostratigraphies, i.e., the phylostrata
marking the transition to a distinct evolutionary regime. The latest breakpoint generally coincides with the
onset of a plateau in GAN frequencies. In most cases, this occurs at the ancestral ORFs or de novo levels
(8/19) or at the TRG level (7/19), suggesting that GAN frequency plateaus early in evolution. The exceptions
consist of H. sapiens and the two plant species (A. thaliana and O. sativa), where the latest breakpoint
occurs slightly later, at Boreoeutheria, Brassicaceae, and Commelinids, respectively.
Figure 4 and S9 have been updated to display the localization of these breakpoints along the GAN kinetics.

“Genome trees for the reconstruction of ancestral sequences and the calculation of ORF conservation
profiles were constructed with OrthoFinder93 version 2.5.5. First, for every focal genome and its neighbors,
we extracted the longest isoform of each gene to produce an amino acid FASTA file per genome. Orthofinder
identifies orthogroups and constructs one unrooted gene tree for each orthogroup using MAFFT94 for

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Roginski et al. examines the impact of GC content on de novo gene birth, an important
topic in gene origination, given that species in different clades may have widely varying GC contents, yet all
likely possess de novo genes in their genomes. The authors identified stop-to-stop intergenic ORFs from
more than 3,000 species, analyzed their hydrophobicity, and used ancestral sequence reconstruction to
study the evolution of ORF hydrophobicity. The topic is both interesting and timely, though it is unclear why
the authors focused solely on HCA scores, given the wide range of ordered and disordered genes in any
given species, and that there is no clear agreement and empirical evidence on whether young de novo
genes are ordered. Below are my comments related to the methods and results.
We would first like to thank the Reviewer for their positive comments and constructive feedback, which we
have fully addressed in our response letter and, where appropriate, in the revised manuscript. Before
addressing the specific comments raised by the Reviewer, we would like to clarify our rationale for using
HCA.
We chose HCA because it is fast and alignment-free, which was crucial for studying millions of fast-evolving
ORFs. Moreover, HCA provides a single score that spans the structural spectrum (from disorder to
aggregation propensities), allowing us to describe the structural properties of a sequence with one unified
metric, rather than relying on multiple tools with distinct outputs (e.g., IUPred23, TANGO24, etc).
aggregation propensities of iORFs with IUPred and TANGO. These results, now presented in Figure S2, are
consistent with the trends predicted by HCA. We observe a positive correlation between disorder
propensity and GC content, and an anticorrelation with aggregation propensity, supporting the hypothesis
that AT-rich genomes contain hydrophobic, aggregation-prone iORFs, while GC-rich ones mostly encode
hydrophilic, disordered iORFs. While these independent tools help corroborate the structural trends
identified with HCA, we remain aware that all of these approaches are computational. However, this
computational framework was essential for exploring such questions across 3,379 eukaryotic genomes,
encompassing broad ranges of GC content, phylogenetic diversity, and lifestyles - something that would be
intractable experimentally. These findings now provide a basis for targeted experimental validation in
selected species, akin to a recent study performed on Drosophila melanogaster and Homo sapiens25.
We included this new analysis in the manuscript:
“As a control, we predicted the disorder and aggregation propensities of iORFs using IUPred58 and TANGO59
(Figure S2A-B). Results align with HCA predictions, showing that disorder propensity positively correlates
with GC content, while aggregation propensity anticorrelates with it. This supports the hypothesis that AT-
rich genomes predominantly encode aggregation-prone iORFs, whereas GC-rich ones encode disordered
ones.”

1) While it is understandable that a straightforward approach to identifying ORFs is through STOP-to-STOP
analysis, these are not truly iORFs. I wonder how the results would differ if the authors used a start-to-stop
criterion for ORF identification. Ideally, having start-to-stop data for all species would be the best approach,
but this may not be feasible within the revision timeframe. I suggest that the authors compare STOP-to-
STOP ORFs with start-to-stop ORFs in a subset of species across different clades to provide insights into the
impact of the methodological approach.
We define iORFs from stop-to-stop, not because it is the most straightforward computationally, but
because growing evidence shows that translation frequently initiates at non-AUG codons, making ATG-
based definitions potentially too restrictive. Multiple studies have demonstrated that translation does not
rely exclusively on canonical ATG start codons (e.g., Slavoff et al.26, Cuevas et al.27, Ingolia et al.28, Na et
al.29, Papadopoulos et al.30, Zheng & Zhao31).
For instance, Slavoff et al.26 reported that in H. sapiens, only 43% of small ORF-encoded peptides start with
ATG, 21% with near-cognate codons, and the remaining 36% with other codons (see Figure 2D in Slavoff et
al.). Similarly, in our previous analyses of Ribo-seq data from S. cerevisiae30, we found that only ~50% of
detected translation events initiate at ATGs. Recently, Zheng & Zhao identified 993 peptides from
unannotated ORFs in D. melanogaster via mass spectrometry, of which only 331 began with canonical start
codons31. Notably, those with and without ATG start shared comparable properties in amino acid
composition and genomic context (e.g., intergenic, UTRs, sense, antisense).
Thus, defining iORFs from stop-to-stop ensures we do not systematically exclude many ORFs that could
initiate translation with non-canonical starts. While this definition may add a short N-terminal extension
that in fact would not be translated (if the ORF were to be translated), unlike canonical CDSs - whose
upstream regions differ markedly from their evolved sequence, iORFs are unevolved and their putative
upstream regions (if translated) are not expected to differ significantly in amino acid composition and
patterning from the rest of the sequence.
Nevertheless, to address the Reviewer’s concern, we re-analyzed the dataset used for the original Figure 2
(based on a representative subset of iORFs from the 3,379 genomes), this time defining iORFs from start-
to-stop (with start = ATG). As shown in Figure D, the overall trends remain consistent: iORFs in AT-rich
species tend to display higher HCA scores, while those from intermediate and GC-rich species show
intermediate and lower scores, respectively. Similarly, the frequencies of positively and negatively charged
residues across genomes are in line with our initial findings using the stop-to-stop definition.
While this complementary analysis confirms the robustness of our findings, we chose not to include it in
the main manuscript to maintain focus, and since the manuscript is already quite lengthy. However, we
remain fully open to providing it as supplementary material should the Editors or Reviewers find it helpful.

3) The authors should provide more details on the detection of de novo genes using DENSE. One major
challenge in identifying de novo genes is distinguishing them from rapidly evolving genes. It may be
beneficial to incorporate methods such as HMMER or foldseek to further exclude potential artefacts.
We thank the Reviewer for this insightful comment regarding fast-evolving genes and acknowledge that
our description of the DENSE pipeline lacked sufficient detail. We have expanded the method section to
better introduce the methodology.
DENSE9 is a two-step procedure. It first identifies gene candidates that are taxonomically restricted, by
default at the genus level. To do so, it relies on GenEra32, which screens with DIAMONDv233 the focal
species’ proteome against the nr database. Each CDS is then assigned an evolutionary age, corresponding
to the most distant node in the NCBI phylogeny where DIAMONDv2 has detected the CDS. In cases where
a gene has multiple isoforms, the age of the oldest one is assigned to all isoforms. For each TRG, it then
tests whether the gene was ancestrally noncoding. Therefore, using TBLASTN, DENSE searches for
homology traces in noncoding regions of outgroup species among the neighbors of the focal species. These
species are those (i) lacking the candidate gene and (ii) branching after the last common ancestor node of
the gene family. To validate TBLASTN hits, DENSE uses microsynteny to confirm that the detected
noncoding hits in outgroup species are located at the same locus as the focal de novo gene candidate.
Candidates with at least one syntenic noncoding hit in two or more outgroup species are retained as
potential candidates and then filtered based on remote or structural homology according to the Reviewer’s
suggestion. Indeed, we fully agree that DIAMONDv2 may fail to detect distant homologs that have diverged
beyond recognition. To mitigate this risk, we implemented a filtering strategy to exclude candidates
potentially corresponding to fast-evolving genes:
On the one hand, we screened all de novo CDS candidates against the Pfam database using HMMER34 (e-
value £ 1x10-3), without applying a coverage threshold, in order to remain conservative - that is, we chose
to eliminate any candidate showing a detectable domain match, regardless of the extent of the match, to
reduce the risk of retaining false positives (i.e., fast-evolving genes that may have retained only partial
domain similarity). Any candidate with a significant match outside the genus of the focal species was
removed from the de novo CDS set. For genes with multiple isoforms, all isoforms were screened. If any

(ii) Several computational and experimental studies have investigated this question. Some
reported AT-rich protogenes enriched in transmembrane domains17. Other experimental
studies demonstrated that de novo proteins could fold into partially ordered 3D structures or
be associated with some folding potential25,42–45. These experimental studies are consistent
with other computational analyses, including our own work on yeast, which, although limited
to a small number of species (e.g., S. cerevisiae, D. melanogaster, O. sativa…), showed that de
novo proteins may harbor folding potential, with some even predicted as well-folded46–49.
Motivated by these analyses, we extended the analysis to a larger scale. Notably, because structural
properties are directly influenced by amino acid composition, which itself is shaped by GC content (at least
in unevolved sequences), we analyzed a comprehensive dataset of eukaryotic genomes (all annotated
genomes in NCBI with an assembly level of at least “scaffold” as available on March 6, 2023), encompassing
a broad range of GC contents.
As explained earlier, we used HCA as our primary metric, since it is fast and alignment-free (which was
critical for large-scale analyses) and provides a single score spanning the structural spectrum from disorder
to aggregation. However, to strengthen our predictions, we have now included two complementary and
independent analyses (TANGO and IUPred), which have corroborated the predictions obtained by HCA.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In their manuscript, “Impact of GC content on de novo gene birth,” Roginski et al. explore the influence of
GC content in non-coding open reading frames on the structure of potentially encoded microproteins.
Notably, as a major merit, their analysis spans an impressive dataset of 3,379 eukaryotic genomes—far
exceeding the scope of previous studies, which have been limited either to specific evolutionary lineages
or to smaller genome sets (e.g., 187 genomes in Basile et al., 2017). For a subset of 22 organisms, they
employ a combination of ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR)—used here more extensively than in
prior work—and a streamlined, custom-built pipeline for de novo gene identification based on their prior
developed tool DENSE. They compare ancestral ORFs with scrambled ORFs. This is the second major merit
of the study, however I would suggest to compare this also with degenerated codons. Additionally, the
authors consciously avoid reliance on 3D structural predictions, which have recently come under scrutiny
for their (lack of) reliability in the context of de novo or random sequences. However, the use of
hydrophobic cluster analysis (HCA) seems somehow questionable for the short ORFs (60 nucleotides, i.e.,
20 amino acids) analysed because it implicietely assumes the presence of secondary structural elements,
or at least the principal capacity of the sequence to form such.
The manuscript itself lacks engagement with foundational literature on the structural characteristics of de
novo proteins and biophysics. In a few cases, the citations do not support what is written, either because
they are reviews or simply not matching. In some instances, the language is overly colorful for a scientific

Notably, regarding the folding potential, we show that iORFs (depending on GC content) can encode
structural building blocks that resemble those found in folded proteins (see next paragraph and new Figure
S2C). These structural building blocks are identified as HCA clusters. The latter have been shown to
correspond to the elementary structural units of folded proteins62,63. The number, size, and composition of
these clusters, along with the intervening linker regions, are integrated into the HCA score, which serves as
a proxy for predicting an ORF’s folding potential62–64. These structural building blocks may not be sufficient
to drive autonomous folding today, but they could facilitate folding in specific contexts (e.g., upon
interaction with partners, oligomerization, or chaperone assistance25), or evolve toward more stable
structures over time through length extension, refinement of residue composition and patterning, or
domain fusion. In this sense, these iORFs host latent structural potential that may be revealed through
molecular interactions, ORF extension and/or amino acid sequence optimization.
Notably, we have now included a new analysis of HCA cluster sizes in iORFs and CDSs across the 3,379
eukaryotic genomes (new Figure S2C). We find that iORFs in intermediate GC-content species encode HCA
clusters with size distributions comparable to those of CDSs, while extreme AT-rich and GC-rich species
deviate in opposite directions (larger and smaller clusters, respectively)(new Figure S2C). This suggests that
intermediate GC-content species harbor a reservoir of iORFs whose sequence composition and organization
confer a higher propensity to adopt or evolve into what might be described as protofolds.
Overall, our results suggest that such proto-structural features are more common in intermediate GC-
content species, which encode iORFs with a better balance of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues (Figures
2A and S2C). In contrast, iORFs in GC-rich or AT-rich species often skew toward disorder-prone (high
hydrophilic residue content) or aggregation-prone sequences (high hydrophobic residue content),
respectively.
Furthermore, while we agree that very short proteins are unlikely to fold independently, in intermediate
GC-content species (35-50% GC), the median iORF length is approximately 30-40 amino acids (depending
on GC content), and ancestral iORFs are even longer, with lengths often exceeding 60 residues (Figure S11),
thereby likely further enhancing their folding potential. Overall, our results suggest that iORFs from
intermediate GC-content species share more characteristics with CDSs (e.g., hydrophobic residue content,
elementary structural units of proteins) than iORFs from species with extreme GC content. These findings
support the hypothesis that this reservoir may include microproteins with the capacity to evolve more
stable structures. Indeed, if selected, their folding potential could further increase through ORF extension,
and/or optimization of amino acid composition and patterning via positive selection, as discussed in Aubel
et al.45.
Altogether, our findings suggest that intermediate GC-content species offer a favorable background for the
emergence of structurally competent novel microproteins, with more balanced amino acid compositions
and appropriate structural motifs.

L208: What is the cause and what is the consequence in the relationship between DNA and protein
material?
We are not entirely sure we have correctly understood the reviewer’s question. If the question concerns
the direction of causality between DNA and protein constraints - that is, who shaped whom - our study does
not aim to resolve this. Instead, our results indicate that protein foldability imposes a strong constraint on
CDSs in eukaryotic species, regardless of their underlying nucleotide composition.
The phrase “reconciliation between DNA and protein constraints” was not intended to imply a
unidirectional causal relationship, but to emphasize the dual requirements that coding sequences must
satisfy: encoding foldable proteins while being composed of nucleotides that vary in GC content.
Notably, our findings suggest that the need to maintain protein foldability may have influenced the
establishment and structure of the genetic code itself. This suggests a co-evolutionary scenario in which
foldability acted as a key constraint, shaping the correspondence between nucleotide triplets and amino
acids, thereby enabling CDSs to meet both DNA and protein-level constraints.
We have revised the corresponding paragraph to clarify this point:

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have implemented most of our comments, and the manuscript now reads more
smoothly and engages more thoroughly with the relevant literature. Technical aspects of the study
have also improved. We only have a few minor, outstanding comments:
Overall, we thank the Reviewer for their positive feedback. We address all the points raised below.
Authors: “Genomes can be broadly subdivided into coding and noncoding regions, conceptually
classified as distinct and impermeable entities.”
1
- The term “subdivided” seems unnecessary; “divided” would suffice. The use of “impermeable” is
problematic, since the study addresses the transitions between coding and noncoding regions.
I suggest:
“Genomic regions can be divided into coding and noncoding regions, conceptually considered as
distinct entities.”
This sentence should also be supported with a citation. While this concerns functionality beyond
coding/noncoding annotation, see Graur et al. 2013, GBE regarding as how distinct annotations can
be.
Our intent in this opening sentence was to introduce the historical and conceptual view of genomes
as composed of two distinct domains (coding and noncoding), before highlighting that recent OMICS
studies have revealed the expression of presumed noncoding regions and, ultimately, a transition
across these boundaries.
We revised the sentence for clarity as follows:
“Genomes can be broadly divided into coding and noncoding regions, conceptually considered as
distinct entities.”
Because this opening statement refers to the traditional way genomes are conceptualized rather
than to debates on genomic functionality (e.g., ENCODE), we prefer not to cite Graur et al. (2013),
which focuses on functional interpretations beyond the intent of this sentence and might risk
confusing the reader.
Authors: “Using computational methods, we showed that yeast intergenic ORFs encode a wide
diversity of structural potentials, including aggregation-prone peptides, and a majority of ORFs with
folding potential. The latter are not necessarily expected to form well-defined 3D structures but
contain elementary structural blocks that may promote folding in specific contexts (e.g., binding with

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Noncoding regions in eukaryotes are extensively expressed and represent a significant source of novel microproteins, some of which become fixed as de novo genes. However, the structural properties of these unevolved products and the features driving their fixation remain poorly understood. Particularly, the influence of nucleotide composition (GC content) on their structural properties and evolutionary trajectories is still unclear. Here, we predict the foldability and sequence properties of millions of microproteins potentially encoded in the noncoding open reading frames (ORFs) of 3,379 eukaryotic genomes with GC contents ranging from 18% to 79%. Depending on GC content, these microproteins exhibit distinct structural properties, suggesting different cellular impacts if non-genic regions are pervasively expressed. Using phylostratigraphy, de novo gene search, and ancestral sequence reconstruction, we trace the evolution of several hundred de novo proteins across 22 organisms with varying GC contents. We show that de novo genes preferentially emerge from GC-rich ORFs with folding potential, revealing that the interplay between GC content and foldability-rooted in the structure of the genetic code-shapes the emergence of novel genes.

---

## Introduction

Genomes can be broadly divided into coding and noncoding regions, conceptually considered as distinct entities. Noncoding regions, which consist of untranslated regions that may play regulatory roles, are primarily constrained at the nucleotide level, such as GC content (i.e., percentage of GC bases), and evolve independently of protein-related constraints. In contrast, coding regions, being translated into functional proteins, must simultaneously satisfy the constraints imposed by both DNA and proteins. Recent studies showed that (i) noncoding regions harbor vast reservoirs of small Open Reading Frames (ORFs) that can be expressed at the protein level, and (ii) the transition from noncoding to coding sequences (CDSs) is possible1–9. Notably, advances in OMIC technologies revealed that regions annotated as noncoding can be transcribed and translated into small proteins, with thousands of microproteins reported across multiple eukaryotic species3,5,10–13. Furthermore, several studies have demonstrated that transitions from noncoding to CDSs are far more common than previously thought6,14,15. Notably, hundreds of newly expressed products have been shown to be functional based on CRISPR-based genetic screens, or shown to undergo selection, thereby establishing them as part of the coding repertoire3,15–19.

De novo gene birth, which refers to the emergence of novel genes from ancestrally noncoding DNA, has been demonstrated to significantly contribute to genome evolution in various eukaryotic species14,15,20–22. Initially considered unlikely due to the stark differences between coding and noncoding regions, de novo genes have garnered increasing attention over the past decade, prompting researchers to elucidate their properties, functions, and mechanisms of emergence. These genes display peculiar characteristics: they have unique amino-acid compositions, are expressed in specific tissues or conditions, and are longer than random ORFs, while shorter than canonical genes6,23–27. Although some features of de novo genes (e.g., short length, weak expression) might also reflect nonfunctional, noisily expressed ORFs, the fact that several display tissue-specific expression28–30, undergo selection15,16,18,19, or have been experimentally shown to be functional19,31–33, supports the view that they can reasonably be classified as coding.

Taken together, these observations establish de novo gene birth as a significant driver of genetic novelty and raise a fundamental question: how does a noncoding sequence become coding? The mechanism of pseudogenization34,35, whereby protein-coding genes revert to noncoding DNA, is easier to grasp since breaking appears simpler than creating. However, de novo gene birth from scratch is harder to envision, especially given the unevolved nature (from a protein perspective) of noncoding sequences. This intriguing question can be reframed in terms of constraints faced by coding and noncoding sequences: how does a noncoding sequence governed only by DNA-level constraints transition to a CDS subject to both DNA and protein-level constraints?

Noncoding regions display distinct nucleotide distributions from coding ones, resulting in different amino-acid patterns if translated23,36. The expression of noncoding regions is, therefore, expected to generate aberrant or harmful proteins rather than functional templates for novel genes. This apparent paradox—how compositionally biased sequences give rise to functional proteins—has stimulated numerous studies, leading to various models of de novo gene birth. The “preadaptation” model posits that only sequences “preadapted” to avoid deleterious effects, such as aggregation, can transition into CDSs37. These de novo proteins, characterized by higher disorder, are therefore well-tolerated by the cell and evolve towards greater structural order over time. However, Tretyachenko et al. showed that random sequences can display secondary structure content and physicochemical properties similar to natural proteins, making them well-tolerated by the cell38. Heames et al. reported hundreds of putative de novo proteins in humans and flies that resemble random sequences in structural potential, though with a higher proportion of soluble and protease-sensitive sequences. Interestingly, their findings suggest that structure-forming potential can emerge from random sequences without prior selection39. In contrast to the preadaptation model, the proto-gene model proposes a gradual transition, where de novo genes evolve from transitory proto-genes arising from pervasive expression of non-genic sequences6. In yeast, de novo proteins were predicted to be less disordered than old ones and expected to acquire greater solubility during evolution. Recently, Tassios et al. reported a widespread potential for transmembrane (TM) domains encoded in intergenic regions of several hundred budding yeast genomes40. Interestingly, Vakirlis et al. found that ORFs with a high TM propensity could be beneficial to Saccharomyces cerevisiae41. The authors proposed a TM-first model, whereby newly translated TM peptides benefit from the membrane environment that prevents them from aggregation, and may later evolve towards greater solubility and broader cellular functions. On the other hand, using computational methods, we showed that yeast intergenic ORFs encode a wide diversity of structural elements, including aggregation-prone peptides, and a majority of ORFs with folding potential23. The latter are not necessarily expected to form well-defined 3D structures on their own but contain elementary structural blocks that may promote folding in specific contexts (e.g., upon binding to a partner or membrane, or through chaperone assistance39) and could support the evolution of more stable structures. Using ancestral sequence reconstruction, we found that the ancestral sequences of yeast de novo genes were enriched in sequences with folding potential. Similar studies in Drosophila melanogaster revealed that a majority of de novo proteins are partially or well-folded according to Alphafold2 predictions25. Interestingly, ancestral sequence analyses indicated that most of the well-folded proteins were likely born well-folded as well. While computational studies on the structural properties of de novo proteins have accumulated23,26,42,43, experimental analyses remain scarce, with only a few de novo proteins structurally characterized44–48. Notably, the yeast Bsc4 and the fly Goddard de novo proteins were shown to fold into partially ordered 3D structures containing secondary structure elements but lacking the stable tertiary structure typical of globular proteins44,47. Collectively, these findings underscore the importance of understanding how protein foldability contributes to the establishment of novel protein-coding genes, while raising questions about their generalizability across species. In particular, protein foldability depends on amino-acid composition, which in turn is influenced by DNA GC content.

In this work, we investigate how GC content impacts (i) the ORF reservoir of an organism and (ii) the transition between noncoding and CDSs. Across 3379 eukaryotic species with various GC contents, we analyze the sequence and structural properties of presumed noncoding ORFs and CDSs. Then, focusing on 22 species, we employ phylostratigraphy, de novo gene search, and ancestral sequence reconstruction to investigate the transitory stages leading to the establishment of canonical proteins. This work reveals (i) GC-content ranges that seem more favorable to de novo gene birth, and (ii) features promoting the emergence of novel genes. Our results support a unified model of de novo gene birth, integrating previous observations through the lens of GC content and specific protein features coordinated by the structure of the genetic code.

---

## Results

Impact of GC content on CDS and iORF codons
We established a dataset of 3379 eukaryotic genomes with GC contents ranging from 17.5 to 78.5% (see Supplementary Data File 1 for the genome list). We extracted their CDSs and all stop-to-stop ORFs of at least 60 nucleotides located in inter-CDS regions (iORFs), since large fractions of microproteins do not start with methionine10,23,49. Consistent with previous studies50, GC content is strongly correlated between CDSs and noncoding regions (Pearson’s r=0.85, p < 1 × 10−16), yet remains systematically higher in CDSs (Fig. S1A). To assess GC effects on the codon frequencies of CDSs, we analyzed the distribution of various codon groups in CDSs and iORFs across the 3379 eukaryotic genomes (Fig. 1A). While some codons display comparable frequencies in CDSs and iORFs, lying on the diagonal (e.g., GTN, CAN, AAN), others appear enriched or depleted in CDSs, lying either above or below the diagonal, respectively (e.g., GCN, GAN, TTN). To discern whether codon frequencies are simply driven by the higher GC content of CDSs or reflect constraints operating at the protein level, we generated scrambled CDSs preserving nucleotide composition but disrupting codons and, consequently, protein-related constraints. Then, to quantify whether differences between real and scrambled CDSs stem solely from protein-level constraints or are also influenced by adaptive codon preferences (i.e., translational selection), we calculated the correlation between GC3 and the GC content of noncoding regions across the 3379 genomes. In line with Bénitière et al.51, we observed a strong correlation (Pearson R2=0.64, r=0.79, p < 1 × 10−16), supporting that codon usage is primarily driven by GC content (Fig. S1B). Figure 1B shows the log fold change (LFC) of each codon group representing the deviation of its frequency in real CDSs compared to scrambled ones. Figure 1C illustrates the variation in its frequency across genomes for iORFs (x-axis) and CDSs (y-axis). Variation is quantified by the standard deviation (SD) of a codon group’s frequency distribution, with high SDs indicating high variability according to GC content, and low SDs indicating more stable frequencies. Codons near the diagonal vary similarly in CDSs and iORFs, whereas those in the middle-right region of the plot (e.g., NTN, NGN) vary widely in iORFs but remain constrained in CDSs (Fig. 1C).

Several codon groups exhibit small LFCs, reflecting similar frequencies in real and scrambled CDSs (Fig. 1B). Notably, mixed AT/GC codons (e.g., TCN, CAN, or GTN) typically show little variation in both iORFs and CDSs (bottom-left corner of Fig. 1C), reflecting low sensitivity to GC content. Overall, most codons have absolute LFCs below 0.5, but four groups show stronger deviations (|LFCs|>0.75): TAN, TGN, CGN, and GAN. Their median frequencies differ significantly from those of scrambled CDSs (Mann–Whitney U test (two-sided), all p < 1 × 10−16) (Fig. S1C). TAN and TGN comprise the three stop codons and the rare amino acids tryptophan and cysteine, explaining their strong depletion in CDSs relative to expectations (Figs. 1B and S1C). CGN codons, which encode arginine, are also markedly depleted (Figs. 1B and S1C). CpG sites, consisting of cytosine followed by guanine, are prone to methylation and are hypermutable because methylated cytosines frequently undergo deamination to thymine52. Such mutations can generate TGN codons, which may introduce deleterious changes and thereby contribute to the observed depletion of CGN codons. GAN codons, encoding aspartate and glutamate, display the highest LFC, and a low frequency variation in CDSs (0.116 ± 0.005) across genomes (Fig. 1B, C). Previous studies showed that high proportions of negative charges on protein surfaces prevent promiscuous interactions with the negatively charged, abundant ribosomes53, and stretches of such residues optimize translation by facilitating the nascent peptide’s passage through the negatively charged ribosomal exit tunnel54. In yeast, we also found a correlation between negative charge frequency and protein abundance, suggesting that a higher frequency of negative charges in abundant proteins may favor their translation efficiency and reduce nonspecific interactions with ribosomes23. Finally, the NTN group, encoding most hydrophobic residues, stands out in Fig. 1C, showing the widest variation in iORFs but constrained frequencies in CDSs (0.27 ± 0.01). This suggests that selection acts to maintain optimal hydrophobicity for protein folding, preserving enough hydrophobic residues in GC-rich species for proper folding while reducing their frequency in AT-rich species to prevent aggregation. This aligns with Dill’s classic theory, which proposed that protein stability depends on an optimal fraction of hydrophobic residues55. Overall, our findings reveal codon groups whose frequencies are tightly regulated to meet protein requirements at any GC content. Interestingly, these properties, ensuring proper foldability, expression, and interactability, together constitute a hallmark of CDSs.

Intermediate GC-content genomes encode microproteins akin to CDSs
Typically, hydrophobic residues are encoded by AT-rich codons, whereas GC-rich codons predominantly encode charged and polar residues. In noncoding regions, where no selection acts on codons, AT-rich and GC-rich sequences are expected to encode preferentially hydrophobic and hydrophilic sequences, respectively. We assessed the foldability of the proteins and microproteins encoded in the CDSs and iORFs of the 3379 genomes using the Hydrophobic Cluster Analysis (HCA) method56–58 (see “Methods”). HCA is fast and does not require multiple sequence alignments, making it ideal for characterizing millions of fast-evolving iORFs. Based on the sole information of the amino acid sequence, HCA identifies (i) clusters of hydrophobic residues, which have been shown to constitute signatures of folded domains, and (ii) hydrophilic linkers connecting clusters and corresponding to loops or disordered regions. From these features, HCA computes a foldability score. Low scores indicate disordered proteins enriched in hydrophilic residues, while high scores correspond to sequences with long hydrophobic clusters, prone to aggregation or forming TM segments. Intermediate HCA scores reflect sequences with balanced proportions of hydrophobic clusters and linkers expected to be associated with folding potential23,58. The latter may either fold into well-defined 3D structures or harbor latent folding potential, i.e., the capacity to adopt structured conformations under specific conditions, and/or evolve more stable structures. Figure 2A represents the HCA scores of iORFs and CDSs according to GC content. We show that GC content has a substantial impact on iORF foldability. AT-rich and GC-rich species predominantly harbor iORFs encoding aggregation-prone or disordered microproteins, respectively, while iORFs of intermediate GC-content genomes tend to display intermediate HCA scores, reflecting a greater folding potential. As a control, we predicted the disorder and aggregation propensities of iORFs using IUPred59 and TANGO60 (Fig. S2A, B). Results align with HCA predictions, showing that disorder propensity positively correlates with GC content, while aggregation propensity anticorrelates with it. This supports the hypothesis that AT-rich genomes predominantly encode aggregation-prone iORFs, whereas GC-rich ones encode disordered ones. Consequently, depending on GC content, iORFs-encoded microproteins may sample distinct structural spaces, potentially generating ensembles with various structural properties and cellular impact if translated. Conversely, although the GC content slightly influences CDS foldability, all genomes generally encode foldable CDSs and display tighter HCA score distributions than iORFs, suggesting foldability as a key constraint in CDSs. This observation highlights the dual pressures imposed by both DNA composition and protein structure and suggests that foldability has played a pivotal role in the establishment of the genetic code, allowing CDSs to maintain foldability regardless of GC content. Finally, we show that in intermediate GC-content species, iORFs and CDSs exhibit similar folding potentials with significant overlaps in their HCA score distributions, whereas in extreme GC-content species, their foldability distributions differ markedly. Previously, we showed that yeast iORFs had HCA cluster sizes similar to CDSs23. To assess the impact of GC content on the size of HCA clusters, we analyzed their size distributions across species. Figure S2C shows that intermediate GC-content iORFs display HCA cluster sizes comparable to CDSs, while extreme AT-rich and GC-rich iORFs deviate in opposite directions (larger and smaller clusters, respectively). This suggests that intermediate GC-content species harbor a reservoir of iORFs potentially encoding the structural building blocks of proteins.

Similar trends are observed for other sequence properties, with CDSs and iORFs in extreme GC-content species exhibiting greater differences in some codon frequencies. In intermediate GC-content species, iORFs display frequencies of codons coding for positively charged residues similar to CDSs, whereas in GC-rich species, these frequencies significantly exceed those of CDSs (Fig. 2B). Although GAN codon distributions in iORFs and CDSs never overlap, the difference between iORF and CDS distributions is much greater in extreme GC-content species (Fig. 2C). Nonetheless, the consistent difference in GAN frequencies between iORFs and CDSs across all genomes suggests that while CDSs display high GAN frequencies, matching these frequencies is not crucial to enter the coding repertoire, and this criterion might be adjusted later in evolution. Finally, as expected, iORF length increases with GC content, due to the AT-richness of stop codons (Fig. S2D).

Overall, these results suggest that, aside from ORF length, iORFs in intermediate GC-content species exhibit sequence and structural characteristics more akin to CDSs than those in extreme GC-content species.

Transition from noncoding to coding sequences
We next investigated the features that could determine de novo gene birth and characterized the evolutionary intermediates leading to canonical proteins. We used DENSE, a fully automated workflow that identifies genes with strong evidence of de novo emergence61. DENSE screens the nr database for taxonomically restricted genes (TRGs) and tests whether they were ancestrally noncoding by searching for homology traces within syntenic orthologous noncoding regions of the outgroup species lacking the gene (see “Methods”). We applied DENSE to 22 well-annotated species (focal species) with well-annotated neighboring species, spanning GC contents from 19% (P. falciparum) to 64.5% (C. reinhardtii) (see Supplementary Data File 2 for the genome list). TRGs were defined at the genus level, except for H. sapiens and M. musculus, where the level was set to “Hominoidea” and “Murinae,” respectively, to ensure enough neighboring species. Table 1 summarizes the number of detected de novo genes and associated CDS isoforms across the 22 genomes. Interestingly, no de novo genes were found in H. opuntiae, and no more than two were identified in extremely AT-rich species (P. falciparum, E. histolytica, and Rotaria sp.).

Ancestral sequence reconstruction is a powerful approach to investigate the properties of the ancestral ORFs that gave rise to de novo genes23,47,62. We reconstructed the ancestral sequences of the identified de novo genes using a protocol inspired by our previous work23, as well as an alternative protocol described in Vakirlis et al.62 to ensure robustness. For each species, Fig. 3A shows the GC content distribution of its iORFs and the ancestral ORFs of its de novo genes. Only species with at least 20 reconstructed ancestral ORFs are shown (see Fig. S3A for the others species). Ancestral ORFs consistently exhibit higher GC content than the other iORFs of the same species (one-sided Mann–Whitney U test, all p < 1 × 10−3, Table S3). This trend persists even in GC-rich species, where ancestral ORFs exceed the already high GC levels of their noncoding regions. Moreover, this pattern also holds for the ancestral ORFs predicted by the PREQUEL-based protocol of Vakirlis et al.62, and for the de novo genes’ orthologous noncoding regions in the first outgroup species where the de novo gene is absent (Figs. S4 and S5). These orthologous noncoding loci also show higher GC contents, further supporting the trend predicted for ancestral sequences. Using GenEra63, a program predicting gene age through phylostratigraphy, we monitored the evolution of GC content over time. For all species, GC content appears to reach a plateau from the first phylostrata and remains strongly constrained throughout all evolutionary intermediates (Figs. 4 and S6). These findings suggest that GC-rich iORFs are more likely to give rise to novel genes, supporting the hypothesis that increased GC content is a key feature of the transition from noncoding to CDSs. However, the observed increase in GC content may also impact the properties of the resulting products, potentially influencing the de novo gene emergence process.

We thus investigated how the GC content of ancestral ORFs affects their structural properties, GAN content, and length. Figure 3B shows the HCA score distributions of the iORFs and ancestral ORFs for each species with more than 20 reconstructed ancestral ORFs (see Fig. S3B for the others species). In many species, ancestral ORFs exhibit distinct foldability from other iORFs, a trend also observed for the ancestral sequences predicted by the PREQUEL-based protocol of Vakirlis et al.62, and the de novo genes’ orthologous noncoding loci in the neighboring species (Figs. S4 and S5). The GC-content increase in ancestral ORFs seems generally associated with a decrease in the HCA scores, except for the most GC-rich species, where the iORF HCA scores are already low (Fig. 3B). This pattern reflects that GC-rich codons predominantly encode hydrophilic or disorder-promoting residues, such as proline and glycine. Nonetheless, ancestral ORFs typically remain within the foldable range of HCA scores, except in H. sapiens and M. musculus, where distributions span disordered and foldable regions due to their substantial GC-content increases. Remarkably, AT-rich species feature a high discrepancy in foldability between their ancestral ORFs and current iORFs, with ancestral ORFs displaying significantly lower HCA scores (Fig. 3B). In highly GC-rich species, ancestral iORFs remain predicted to harbor folding potential despite their GC-content increase, normally expected to promote local disorder. To determine whether ancestral ORF foldability stems solely from their GC content or is a selected trait, we scrambled their nucleotides, preserving GC content while disrupting codons and, therefore, protein-level constraints. The foldability of scrambled sequences, thus, represent the expectation based only on nucleotide composition. In several species with high levels of AT or GC (e.g., A. thaliana, S. cerevisiae, and L. infantum), ancestral ORFs show significantly different HCA scores from their scrambled counterparts. Specifically, L. infantum’s ancestral ORFs have higher HCA scores than their scrambled counterparts, while most AT-rich species shift toward higher local disorder, though remaining within the foldable bin (Figs. 3B and S3B). This suggests that selection retained iORFs with a certain level of foldability, specifically under extreme GC contexts, where foldable iORFs arise less frequently. Depending on their nucleotide composition, ancestral ORFs exhibit specific codon distributions that either further amplify the GC-content effect in AT-rich species or buffer it in GC-rich ones (Fig. S7). Specifically, ancestral ORFs from GC-rich species are usually enriched in cysteines and consistently depleted in disorder-promoting residues (glycine and proline) compared to their scrambled counterparts, potentially enhancing their folding potential. Conversely, ancestral ORFs from AT-rich species are generally depleted in hydrophobic residues and enriched in glycines and prolines, potentially promoting local disorder and solubility. This is clearly illustrated by the principal component analysis of their amino-acid propensities, which clusters species by GC content, except Plasmodium vivax, which stands apart and, interestingly, is associated with 42% GC but was ancestrally AT-rich (Fig. S7). Finally, HCA scores across phylostrata reveal that although young phylostrata (TRGs), including de novo genes, are generally predicted with folding potential, their foldability varies significantly depending on the species’ GC content (Figs. 4 and S8B, C). In contrast, older phylostrata (Eukaryotes and Cellular organisms) display lower variations in their HCA scores irrespective of species’ GC contents (F-test, p = 6.2 × 10−6) (Fig. S8C).

No clear pattern emerges in GAN codon frequency distributions of ancestral ORFs. In most species, their GAN frequency is similar to that of their scrambled sequences and that of iORFs, supporting our hypothesis that GAN frequency is not critical in the early stages of de novo gene birth (Fig. S3C). Although GAN codons may influence translation efficiency and protein interactability, de novo microproteins are typically expressed at low levels21, minimizing their immediate cellular impact. Nonetheless, our evolutionary kinetics reveal a rapid adjustment of GAN frequency, as shown with the red arrows indicating transitions to distinct evolutionary regimes (see “Methods”) (Figs. 4 and S9). The latest transition generally coincides with the onset of a plateau in GAN frequencies, usually reached at the ancestral ORFs or de novo gene levels (8/19) or at the TRG level (7/19), suggesting that GAN frequency stabilizes early in evolution. Finally, consistent with prior studies20,23,64,65, ancestral ORFs are significantly longer than other iORFs, regardless of GC content, and longer than their scrambled counterparts (Figs. 4, S10 and S11), suggesting that their increased size reflects a selected criterion rather than resulting solely from higher GC content. Moreover, in line with previous studies6,22,66,67, we confirm that CDS size evolution is a continuous process, as evidenced by the increase in ORF size across phylostrata (Figs. 4 and S10).

GC content in relation to de novo gene counts
AT-rich and GC-rich species appear to harbor fewer de novo genes than intermediate-GC species. We first examined whether technical factors could bias de novo gene detection. We searched for the divergence time for each focal species and its nearest neighbor from TimeTree68 or the literature69 (Table 1). For most species, including P. falciparum, P. vivax, and E. histolytica, which have very few detected de novo genes, divergence times are short (<6–7 Mya). Interestingly, H. opuntiae harbors only 27 orphans, despite a long divergence time with its neighbor (41 Mya), showing that interpreting patterns of molecular innovation from divergence time is complex and may be inaccurate when comparing species with different generation times and evolutionary rates. To further assess the genomic distance between focal species and their neighbors, we analyzed the homology profiles of noncoding segments across each focal species’ neighbors to see whether species with few de novo genes were associated with poor homology signals61 (Fig. S12). Species with few de novo genes were not consistently linked to poor homology profiles: E. histolytica and Rotaria sp. have only one de novo gene despite homology profiles similar to A. thaliana (99 de novo genes), whereas C. javanica harbors 63 de novo genes despite a poor homology detectability. Additionally, low-complexity sequences, frequent in extreme GC-content genomes, may also weaken homology signals between de novo candidates and their orthologous noncoding regions in the neighbors. However, Fig. S13 shows that amino-acid sequences of extreme GC-content species display complexity comparable to those of other species. These findings suggest that although technical factors may influence de novo gene detection, they alone cannot explain the low de novo gene counts observed for AT- and GC-rich species.

We, thus, investigated biological features that might underlie the discrepancies in the number of de novo genes across the 22 species. Most AT- and GC-rich species are parasitic or opportunistic and, as typical for parasites, have small genomes (<10,000 genes). The three exceptions are Rotaria sp., T. versicolor, and C. reinhardtii, which are free-living organisms with large gene repertoires despite few de novo genes. AT-rich species seem to contain even fewer de novo genes than GC-rich ones, potentially due to their more extreme GC content (20–30%) compared to the most GC-rich species, C. reinhardtii (64.5%). Furthermore, aggregation, being more detrimental than disorder, may also influence innovation strategies in extreme AT-rich species. P. falciparum displays high recombination rates in subtelomeric antigen families, generating antigenic diversity70,71. E. histolytica shows evidence of bacterial gene acquisition through horizontal gene transfer (HGT)72, and harbors abundant retrotransposons implicated in genome rearrangements73. Finally, Rotaria sp. exhibits frequent HGTs from non-metazoan sources74.

We next examined whether a phylogenetic signal exists across the 3379 species based on their GC content (Table S6). GC-rich species mostly consist of Fungi (82%), with the remaining species belonging to SAR (8%), Chlorophytes (4%), and Discoba (3.5%). In contrast, AT-rich species are more widely distributed across the tree of life, with 67% Opisthokontes (mainly Arthropods, Nematodes, and Fungi), 22% Streptophytes, and 7% SAR (almost all Apicomplexa). Intermediate GC-content species display a distinct pattern, dominated by Opisthokontes (88%)—split between Metazoa (57%) and Fungi (43%), and small proportions of Streptophytes (9%) and SAR (3%). Finally, we investigated the relationship between genome size and GC content, revealing two genome-size populations across the 3379 genomes (Fig. S14). Large genomes (>1000 Mbp) are mostly found in intermediate GC-content species, whereas GC-rich species typically have small genomes (<100 Mbp). Unlike GC-rich species, AT-rich species feature a broader range of genome sizes, with Arthropods and Nematodes associated with larger genomes, while Fungi and Apicomplexa display smaller genomes. Overall, although we observe a relationship between species phylogenetic distribution and GC content, and extreme GC-content species tend to have fewer de novo candidates, these patterns do not directly match genome size and lifestyle. Some parasites (e.g., C. javanica, L. infantum) possess many de novo genes, whereas some large-genome species have few (e.g., Rotaria sp., T. versicolor, C. reinhardtii). Conversely, small genomes, such as that of S. cerevisiae, still contain many de novo genes, highlighting a complex relationship between these factors. Altogether, these results provide a basis for future studies on how lifestyle, phylogeny, and GC content influence de novo gene emergence and whether GC content limits the ability of some species to evolve through de novo gene birth.

---

## Methods

Collection of CDSs and iORFs
From the NCBI genomes datasets (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/datasets/genome/), we selected all the annotated genomes with an assembly level of at least “scaffold” (contig < scaffold < chromosome < complete) as available on the 6th of March 2023. We kept only one genome per organism name (see Supplementary Data File 1 for the list of genomes). To that aim, we prioritize genomes sharing the same organism’s name as follows (decreasing priority): (1) reference/representative genome, (2) highest assembly level, (3) most recent publication date, (4) highest N50. The CDSs were directly extracted from the CDS FASTA files available on the NCBI. The iORFs were defined from stop-to-stop using the ORFtrack program from the ORFmine package88 (default parameters: 60 nucleotides, iORFs do not overlap any annotated feature (e.g., tRNA, rRNA, CDS…) by more than 70% of their length). To limit computational storage and calculations, Fig. 2 and S2 were generated using randomly selected subsets of 1000 CDSs and 1000 iORFs per genome. Similarly, the iORF distributions of the different features investigated in Figs. 3, 4, S3–S6, S8–S10 and S15 were calculated for 1000 randomly selected iORFs.

Detection of de novo genes
The prediction of de novo genes was realized using DENSE61 version 1.0.8. DENSE was run with default parameters, except for the number of outgroup species, which was set to “2.” DENSE first identifies TRGs using GenEra63. The TRG rank was set to “genus” for all species except for H. sapiens and M. musculus, where it was set to “Hominoidea” and “Murinae,” respectively, to ensure a minimum number of neighbors. For each TRG, it then tests whether the gene was ancestrally noncoding. Therefore, using TBLASTN, DENSE searches for homology traces in noncoding regions of outgroup species among the neighbors of the focal species. These species are those (i) lacking the candidate gene and (ii) branching after the last common ancestor node of the gene family. To validate TBLASTN hits, DENSE uses microsynteny to confirm that the detected noncoding hits in outgroup species are located at the same locus as the focal de novo gene candidate. Candidates with one syntenic noncoding hit in two or more outgroup species are then retained for the next filtering step. DIAMONDv281 may miss distant homologs that have diverged beyond recognition. To mitigate this risk, we screened the retained candidates against the Pfam database using HMMER89 (e value ≤ 1 × 10−3). Candidates with significant matches outside the genus of the focal species were removed from the de novo candidate set. For genes with multiple isoforms, all isoforms were screened. If any isoform yielded a significant match, the gene and its isoforms were conservatively excluded. This step eliminated 15 candidates. We also predicted the 3D structure of each de novo protein candidate using ESMFold90 and searched for structural homologs among the 15 million AlphafoldDB cluster representatives91 with Foldseek92 (e value ≤ 1 × 10−2). Of 10 matches, five overlapped the HMMER-filtered set. The remaining five had Foldseek TM-scores < 0.5, indicating weak structural alignment. TM-scores were reassessed with TM-align93, which is more accurate. One of them yielded a significant TM-score (0.64) and was conservatively removed as well. Links to the used genomes and their annotation are provided in Supplementary Data File 2.

Phylogenetic trees
Genome trees for the reconstruction of ancestral sequences and the calculation of ORF conservation profiles were constructed with OrthoFinder94 version 2.5.5. First, for every focal genome and its neighbors, we extracted the longest isoform of each gene to produce an amino acid FASTA file per genome. Orthofinder identifies orthogroups and constructs one unrooted gene tree for each orthogroup using MAFFT95 for alignments and FastTree96 for tree inference. It then produces a single unrooted species tree with STAG, subsequently rooted with STRIDE through gene tree reconciliation. The command used was “docker run davidemms/orthofinder:2.5.5.2 orthofinder -f <directory_with_input_fasta_files> -t 90 -a 4 -M msa -T fasttree -A mafft.”

Reconstructing the ancestral sequences that gave rise to de novo genes
For each de novo CDS, the DENSE workflow retrieves its best matches across the neighbor genomes that can be either coding or noncoding if no homologous CDS is found. De novo CDSs were then aligned with these homologous sequences. All aligned sequences were previously extended by 99 nucleotides upstream and downstream to include the genomic context, particularly in the case of start or stop displacement. These alignments were generated using MACSE97 version 2.07. Finally, the ancestral sequences were reconstructed using the PRANK98 program version 170427 (e.g., «prank -d=aligned.fna -t=phyml_tree.nwk -o=ouput -once -showanc -prunetree -keep”). As a control, we also applied the ancestral sequence reconstruction method PREQUEL from the PHAST99 package following the same protocol as published in Vakirlis et al.62. For both protocols, we then extracted the ancestral sequence corresponding to the most recent common ancestor between the focal sequence and the first noncoding outgroup. The presence of the second outgroup, therefore, strengthens the confidence in the inference of the ancestral state. From the three frames of the reconstructed ancestral sequences, we then extracted all ORFs defined stop-to-stop of at least 60 nucleotides. Finally, we established an optimal Smith-Waterman100 search of each ancestral ORF with the focal de novo CDS to determine those that actually gave rise to the gene of interest. This search was performed using the ssearch36 program101 (e value ≤ 1 × 10−3).

Scrambled and random sequences
Scrambled CDSs were generated by shuffling their nucleotides. To prevent any internal stop codons, when a stop codon was generated by blending, the codon and the four surrounding codons (five upstream and five downstream) were blended together to minimize bias towards codons similar to stop codons (i.e., sharing stop codons’ nucleotides). To increase statistical power, 1000 scrambled sequences were generated for each species. To compare the size of ancestral ORFs with random sequences of the same GC content (Fig. S11), we generated for each GC percentage bin (0.5%) a random DNA sequence of one million nucleotides long, spanning a range of 0% to 100% GC content. We then extracted the ORFs (≥ 20 codons) from each of these sequences. For each set of ancestral ORFs, we used, as a control, the corresponding set of ORFs with the closest GC content.

GC and HCA distributions of the noncoding regions of the first outgroup species orthologous to the predicted de novo genes
One thousand iORFs were drawn from the species that constitute the first outgroup of each detected de novo gene. These species are represented in proportion to the frequency with which they serve as the first outgroup (e.g., 200 iORFs from species X if species X is the first outgroup in 20% of cases). Orthologous intergenic regions were provided by DENSE as the intergenic regions in the first outgroup species associated with the best TBLASTN102 alignment with a given de novo CDS. We then identified the ORFs within these orthologous intergenic regions that align with the focal CDS (e value ≤ 1 × 10−3) and calculated their HCA scores. The calculation of the GC content of the orthologous noncoding region was performed on the region that aligned through TBLASTN with the nucleotide sequence of the input de novo genes.

Phylostratigraphy and subsequent analyses
The age of each CDS of every focal genome was extracted from the GenEra63 results produced during the execution of DENSE. GenEra63 screens each focal species’ proteome with DIAMONDv281 against the NCBI non-redundant protein database (downloaded on March 28, 2022). Based on the presence/absence of each CDS in the NCBI phylogeny, the CDS is then assigned an evolutionary age. The latter corresponds to the most distant node in the phylogeny where DIAMONDv2 has detected the CDS. If a gene has multiple isoforms, the isoforms are assigned the age of the oldest isoform.

To detect breakpoints (i.e., transitions) in GAN phylostratigraphies, we computed for each species the median GAN codon frequency of each phylostratum. We then fitted three Bayesian piecewise-linear models (null: no change, one breakpoint, and two breakpoints) using the mcp package103. Model performance was evaluated by leave-one-out cross-validation104, extracting the expected log-predictive density (ELPD) and its standard error. Pairwise ELPD differences were calculated, and a more complex model (e.g., two breakpoints over one breakpoint, or one breakpoint over the null model) was accepted only if its improvement (ΔELPD) exceeded the standard error. Posterior mean breakpoints were then extracted from the model estimates and mapped back onto the corresponding phylostrata.

Inter-CDS and intergenic regions
Inter-CDS and intergenic regions were respectively obtained by subtracting all the “CDS” and “genes” intervals from the whole genome GFF, using BEDTOOLS version 2.30.0105 (bedtools subtract).

Conservation profiles
Conservation profiles are made of three columns that reflect the conservation across the neighbors of each focal species: (1) the CDS of de novo genes, (2) a random subset of 1000 intergenic segments, and (3) 1000 randomly selected CDSs that were not predicted as de novo. CDSs of de novo genes: Percentage of de novo CDSs with a coding hit in each neighbor species (BLASTP, e value ≤ 1 × 10−3, query coverage by subject ≥ 50%). Noncoding segments: 1000 intergenic segments of 100 codons were randomly selected from each focal species. The percentage of intergenic segments with a hit in each neighboring species was then estimated using TBLASTN (e value ≤ 1 × 10−3, query coverage by subject ≥ 50%). CDSs: 1000 CDSs were randomly selected from each focal species. The percentage of CDSs with a coding hit in each neighboring species was then estimated using BLASTP (e value ≤ 1 × 10−3, query coverage by subject ≥ 50%).

Calculation of sequence descriptors
Sequence size and GC composition were determined using the faSize and faCount programs from the UCSC utilities (https://hgdownload.cse.ucsc.edu/admin/exe/linux.x86_64/). Codon composition was determined using the R package coRdon (https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/coRdon.html). The HCA score was calculated using the ORFold program from the ORFmine suite57,58,88. Aggregation propensity was assessed with TANGO60. Following Linding et al.60, residues within segments of more than five consecutive residues predicted to adopt a β-aggregated conformation (probability > 5%) were considered aggregation-prone. Sequence aggregation propensity was defined as the fraction of residues in such segments. Disorder propensity was evaluated with IUPred59 using the short prediction option. Residues in segments of more than 5 consecutive residues with disorder probability higher than 0.5 were considered disordered. Disorder propensity was calculated as the fraction of residues in these segments.

Identification of young iORFs under selection in S. cerevisiae
We screened all S. cerevisiae iORFs against the full set of iORFs of its five neighbors using DIAMONDv2 (e value ≤ 1 × 10−3 and coverage ≥ 70%) and retained those with significant matches in at least four neighbors. These sequences were aligned with MAFFT and tested for signature of selection using multiple CODEML branch models (from PAML106 package), following Zhang et al.107, but with a distinct subset of trees for the two-ratio models. This subset included all three versions where a single branch or clade was labeled with a distinct ratio. Chi-squared test p values were Bonferroni-corrected, with significance set at 0.05. Candidates showing signatures of selection were then screened with BLASTP and TBLASTN against the 332 yeast species from Shen et al.108. We removed those with evidence of likely ancient origin, defined as either significant BLASTP matches (e value ≤ 1 × 10−3 and coverage ≥ 70%) or TBLASTN hits with ORF intactness ≥ 70%.

Statistical analyses
Statistical analysis and graphics (ggplot2 (Wickham 2016)) were produced with R version 4.3.2 (2023-10-31)109. Figure S2 involves median comparisons between bins comprising several sets of 1000 ORFs. To address p value issues with large samples, we empirically estimated p values using an iterative sampling approach. For each comparison, we computed the observed median difference (Dobs). We then drew 10,000 random samples of 1000 individuals from each bin being compared and combined them. In each iteration, the pooled sample was split into two equal subsamples to calculate the associated median difference (Dsamp). The p value was defined as the proportion of Dsamp values exceeding Dobs. Boxplots in Figs. 3, 4, S1, S3–S6, S8–S10, S13 and S15 show the median (center line), first and third quartiles (bounds of box), and whiskers extending to the most extreme data points within 1.5 × the interquartile range (IQR): points beyond are outliers. Notches in Figs. 2 and S2 indicate an approximate 95% confidence interval for the median (1.58 × IQR/√n).
