### Reviewer 1

In this manuscript Roginski, Papadopoulos and Lopes present a broad computational analysis of intergenic ORFs across thousands of genomes and then de novo genes and their evolution across 22 eukaryotic lineages. Multiple findings are noteworthy, but what stands out is how GC% seems to influence and constrain the potential for de novo gene emergence and the structural properties of the resulting de novo proteins. The manuscript encompasses an impressive amount of methodologically sound and careful work and is overall very well written. This work will have substantial impact on the field of novel gene evolution, and will no doubt leave a significant mark in the field of genome biology more generally. The authors beautifully build on their previous work in budding yeast and use cutting edge tools that they have developed to present a comprehensive comparison across many species. The scope and depth of the comparison and the fact that it focuses, among others, on the link between genetic code and protein structure makes this work particularly novel. I've listed my comments and some concerns below which I am sure the authors can address to make an already strong manuscript even stronger.
1) It's important to back up as much as possible the claim that very GC-rich and very GC-poor outliers have less de novo genes. Several points to do that:
- I understand that in Table 1, the CDS column contains all isoforms, since we see a value of 143,864 for human. Does the de novo CDS column also contain all isoforms? This should in any case be clarified in the text. It is important because it can bias downstream analyses.
- It should be clear in the text that the TRGs are defined at the genus-level (if this is the case, and unless it's there already and I missed it) and that de novo genes are always species-specific. It also seems that the TRGs do not contain all isoforms, which seems a bit strange but maybe there's a reason, it would be good to have some clarification.
- To further support the link between GC and de novo gene emergence, the authors could also include the numbers of all species-specific genes, not just the ones with de novo evidence. One might expect the trend to hold, especially for those species with close phylogenetic neighbors, where we don't expect many novel genes due to extreme divergence. This could also further show that detectability of orthologous noncoding regions is not an issue.
- The authors could control for other factors that could explain/confound the difference in number of de novo genes. For example, free-living versus parasitic lifestyle (and potentially other organismal traits), evolutionary distance to closest neighbor, genome size and total number of genes. The list of the 22 species contains very different organisms with a range of genome properties. For example, do insects with a similar size genome as Dmel but extreme GC% have lower de novo genes, or even just species-specific genes? (maybe useful https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10978632/) . I leave it up to the authors how much they would like to do on this point, as this could also be future work. In that case, it would be useful to include such potentially confounding factors in the discussion.
2) The finding that ancestral iORFs of de novo genes have higher GC (and that they are longer) than average is a key finding. However there is an important parameter involved, and that is the process of gene finding and annotation, by which these CDSs have been identified as CDSs. Could it be that the way that genes are identified in these genomes biases them towards resembling known, conserved coding sequence GC%, i.e. ORFs that have too low GC% compared to known, conserved genes have a very low chance of being included in gene catalogues in the first place. This can artificially result in the following: out of, say, 100 de novo species-specific CDSs that truly exist in a genome, only the top 50 in terms of GC% will be called by the annotation pipeline, the rest will not be identified as genes. This in turn will mean that when the ancestral ORFs of these CDSs are examined, they will have higher GC% on average than all the other iORFs because they were detected based on that. The same bias could explain the Vakirlis et al. 2018 results as well. I would like an argument by the authors against this, or some analysis that shows that this is not the case. Alternatively this possibility could be presented in the discussion.
On the same point, the authors write on l. 404 "iORFs, which gave rise to novel genes, are distinct from typical iORFs. They form a unique population characterized by higher GC content..."
I think the adjectives "distinct" and "unique" do not reflect the data here. Sure the distributions show clear differences, but there is still overlap. I would suggest using something milder.
3) l. 66 "These observations clearly demonstrate that despite their singularities, these newly emerged genes can unequivocally be classified as coding"
It is important to also note that some of the features of de novo genes (i.e. short length, weak expression) can also be interpreted as them being spurious, "noisily" expressed ORFs, and so this needs to be considered.
4) Figure 1 and associated analysis and comparison of codon frequencies and GCs. I have no doubt about the conclusions here, but some statistics are missing to back up the comments the authors make about the various comparisons, since some of the differences are not that clearly visible by just looking at the figure.
5) l. 365: "Accordingly, older phylostrata converge toward more homogeneous HCA values despite significant variations in GC contents in the corresponding CDSs"
I'm not sure I see that on the plot. Can this evolution of variability be statistically tested so that it's more convincing?
6) l. 374 "Nonetheless, our evolutionary kinetics revealed a rapid adjustment of GAN codon frequency from the youngest phylostrata"
Again, statistical comparison between younger and older phylostrata is needed to support this, even if it seems to be true by looking at Figure S9.
7) Some methodological questions, to be clarified in the text if needed.
- For de novo gene detection, are the outgroups always 2, or at least 2?
- Some additional details in the section "Phylogenetic trees" would be helpful.
- Phylostratigraphy section: please provide a brief description about how GenEra works for the non-specialist reader.
- "Inter-CDS and intergenic regions": Are other genomic elements, apart from CDSs, eg. transposable elements, ncRNA genes etc. included in the sequences that remain after the subtraction? If so, could this be affecting the iORFs in some species more than others?
8) In Figure 5A, I'm not sure I understand the arrows. There is a pink arrow named "codon selection" that points to ancestral iORFs, which I find confusing. Some details in the legend about how to interpret this would be very helpful.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript by Roginski et al. examines the impact of GC content on de novo gene birth, an important topic in gene origination, given that species in different clades may have widely varying GC contents, yet all likely possess de novo genes in their genomes. The authors identified stop-to-stop intergenic ORFs from more than 3,000 species, analyzed their hydrophobicity, and used ancestral sequence reconstruction to study the evolution of ORF hydrophobicity. The topic is both interesting and timely, though it is unclear why the authors focused solely on HCA scores, given the wide range of ordered and disordered genes in any given species, and that there is no clear agreement and empirical evidence on whether young de novo genes are ordered. Below are my comments related to the methods and results.
Major Comments
1) While it is understandable that a straightforward approach to identifying ORFs is through STOP-to-STOP analysis, these are not truly iORFs. I wonder how the results would differ if the authors used a start-to-stop criterion for ORF identification. Ideally, having start-to-stop data for all species would be the best approach, but this may not be feasible within the revision timeframe. I suggest that the authors compare STOP-to-STOP ORFs with start-to-stop ORFs in a subset of species across different clades to provide insights into the impact of the methodological approach.
2) In addition to concerns regarding STOP-to-STOP ORFs, I am curious about how GC content influences the origin and occurrence of ATG—the primary start codon in the vast majority of species.
3) The authors should provide more details on the detection of de novo genes using DENSE. One major challenge in identifying de novo genes is distinguishing them from rapidly evolving genes. It may be beneficial to incorporate methods such as HMMER or foldseek to further exclude potential artefacts.
4) The presentation of Figure 1 is somewhat unclear, though I believe I have understood its intended meaning. Comparisons between CDSs, iORFs, and scrambled sequences may all be significantly different—if so, what is the significance of these differences? Lines 148–181 may contain results related to Figure 1. However, without clear panel separations within the figure, it is difficult to interpret these paragraphs in relation to the data presented fully. Providing clearer figure annotations or structured panel divisions would enhance readability.
5) Figure 2A is very interesting. It shows that there is a strong constraint on HCA scores in the long-term evolution of genes —though not the outliers. I wonder, for the de novo CDS identified in Table 1, what are the HCA scores for de novo CDS with very high and very low GC contents? Comparing the extremes to the annotated CDSs may provide insights into whether there are HCA constraints for de novo genes during birth or whether the HCAs change gradually after gene birth.
6) In Figure 3A, the authors found that ancestral iORFs consistently exhibit higher GC content than other iORFs in the analyzed species, which is consistent with a previously published study. However, this is an unusual result that is difficult to explain biologically and may instead be a computational artefact. I strongly recommend that the authors use at least one additional method for ancestral sequence reconstruction to assess the robustness of these findings.
7) In the paper the authors used HCA scores as a major parameter important for evolution as well as gene origination, as indicated in several figures as well as in figure 5A. However, there is no clear evidence that a functional novel gene needs to be folded, especially at the early stage.
Minor Comments
Line 70: In the section titled “How do we pass from one world to another”, the intended meaning is unclear. The use of the term “world” is somewhat confusing, as there is no distinct separation between different worlds in the context of gene birth, particularly concerning the reservoir of genes.
Lines 86-94: Many proto-genes tend to be AT-rich, especially given that transmembrane domains often originate in T-rich or AT-rich regions, as these regions are more likely to generate amino acids with high hydrophobicity. How does this reconcile with the authors' observations?
Line 214-217, if the raised question not answered, it should belong to discussion.
Lines 561-564: The authors' approach of blending surrounding codons to prevent internal stop codons in scrambled sequences is commendable. However, does blending with four codons introduce any bias in codon composition within these regions?
The readability of the manuscript can be improved. Specifically, figure and figure panels can be cited more rigorously. Some result sections contain guesses and open questions which belong to the discussion.

### Reviewer 3

In their manuscript, “Impact of GC content on de novo gene birth,” Roginski et al. explore the influence of GC content in non- coding open reading frames on the structure of potentially encoded microproteins. Notably, as a major merit, their analysis spans an impressive dataset of 3,379 eukaryotic genomes—far exceeding the scope of previous studies, which have been limited either to specific evolutionary lineages or to smaller genome sets (e.g., 187 genomes in Basile et al., 2017). For a subset of 22 organisms, they employ a combination of ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR)—used here more extensively than in prior work—and a streamlined, custom-built pipeline for de novo gene identification based on their prior developed tool DENSE. They compare ancestral ORFs with scrambled ORFs. This is the second major merit of the study, however I would suggest to compare this also with degenerated codons. Additionally, the authors consciously avoid reliance on 3D structural predictions, which have recently come under scrutiny for their (lack of) reliability in the context of de novo or random sequences. However, the use of hydrophobic cluster analysis (HCA) seems somehow questionable for the short ORFs (60 nucleotides, i.e., 20 amino acids) analysed because it implicietely assumes the presence of secondary structural elements, or at least the principal capacity of the sequence to form such.
The manuscript itself lacks engagement with foundational literature on the structural characteristics of de novo proteins and biophysics. In a few cases, the citations do not support what is written, either because they are reviews or simply not matching. In some instances, the language is overly colorful for a scientific article, and certain metaphors or illustrative phrases do not add clarity but instead may detract from the manuscript’s overall tone.
In the following, I am suggesting changes line-by-line:

L29: What is actually meant by “the nature of the associated evolutionary stages”?

L43: Use “conceptually classified” instead of “long viewed” to highlight the conceptual aspect.
L42–55: The use of words such as “materials” and “worlds” is not scientific and is uncommon.
It impedes readability and does not seem as conceptually intriguing as it was possibly intended to be.
L49: Refer to Grandchamp et al. 2023 & 2024, and Iyengar & Bornberg-Bauer 2023 regarding the transition from non-coding to coding.
L53: “Domains” can be misunderstood. Is it in the sense of Pfam?

This paper is explicit on selection and methodological limits to detect selection in the context.

Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript Roginski, Papadopoulos and Lopes present a broad computational analysis of intergenic
ORFs across thousands of genomes and then de novo genes and their evolution across 22 eukaryotic
lineages. Multiple findings are noteworthy, but what stands out is how GC% seems to influence and
constrain the potential for de novo gene emergence and the structural properties of the resulting de novo
proteins. The manuscript encompasses an impressive amount of methodologically sound and careful work
and is overall very well written. This work will have substantial impact on the field of novel gene evolution,
and will no doubt leave a significant mark in the field of genome biology more generally. The authors
beautifully build on their previous work in budding yeast and use cutting edge tools that they have
developed to present a comprehensive comparison across many species. The scope and depth of the
comparison and the fact that it focuses, among others, on the link between genetic code and protein
structure makes this work particularly novel. I've listed my comments and some concerns below which I am
sure the authors can address to make an already strong manuscript even stronger.

The relationship between orphan gene counts and potentially undetected de novo genes is not
straightforward, as it is influenced by multiple factors. For instance, the number of orphan genes is expected
to depend on the phylogenetic distance between each focal species and its closest relative. As suggested
by the Reviewer, we searched for the divergence times for each focal species and its nearest neighbor from
TimeTree1 or the literature2, and added this information when available to Table 1. The observed patterns
vary, reflecting the difficulty in interpreting the number of orphan genes.
For instance, Drosophila melanogaster exhibits few orphan genes (28) but many taxonomically restricted
genes (966), likely due to its closest relative, which diverged only ~4.6 Mya. This short evolutionary distance
is also supported by a remarkable detectable homology across their respective noncoding regions, as shown
by the noncoding segment homology profile calculated for D. melanogaster and its neighboring species
(Figure S12).
On the other hand, some AT- or GC-rich species with few de novo candidates (such as P. falciparum, E.
histolytica, M. restricta, T. caries, and Rhodotorula sp.) also have relatively few orphan genes, supporting
the hypothesis that de novo genes are indeed rare in these species. In contrast, other AT- or GC-rich species
like P. macacae, Rotaria sp., T. versicolor, and C. reinhardtii harbor many orphans (Table 1). However, the
4
high orphan counts do not necessarily indicate undetected de novo genes, but may instead point to
alternative mechanisms such as horizontal gene transfer (HGT), retrotransposition, or structural genome
rearrangements, that can generate orphan gene gains independently of de novo emergence.
For example:
Pneumocystis species have expanded several gene families (e.g., msg-A1, A3, D), with strong host-specific
diversification, reflecting rapid adaptation to mammalian hosts through gene duplication and diversification
rather than de novo emergence3.
Rotaria species (bdelloid rotifers) show extensive HGT from bacteria, fungi, and protists, with estimates
suggesting that 10–15% of their genes are of non-metazoan origin, making HGT a major source of their
orphan gene content4,5.
C. reinhardtii exhibits a highly dynamic genome characterized by frequent transposon activity, structural
variation, and numerous retrogenes, all of which offer alternative mechanisms for generating novel genes
beyond de novo birth6–8.
While the respective contribution of these aforementioned mechanisms remains challenging to quantify,
we caution against interpreting orphan counts as direct proxies for undetected de novo gene count
estimates, especially in taxa where alternative gene innovation mechanisms exist. This important question
is now examined and presented along with our response to the next Reviewer’s comment in a new Results
section of the manuscript (see next comment).

We first examined whether technical factors could bias de novo gene detection. Specifically, we searched
for the divergence time of each focal species and its nearest neighbor from TimeTree1 or the literature2
when available. Except for H. opuntiae and C. elegans, divergence times with the focal species’ closest
neighbors are typically short (< 6-7 Mya). This also applies to P. falciparum, P. vivax, and E. histolytica, for
which we were able to detect only very few de novo genes. The divergence time for H. opuntiae is much
longer (41 Mya). Although this could have explained our difficulty in detecting de novo genes in H. opuntiae,
the species has only 27 orphan genes, showing that interpreting patterns of molecular innovation from
divergence time is complex and may be inaccurate when comparing species with different generation times
and evolutionary rates.

As suggested by the Reviewer, we searched for other insect species with high AT or GC content to assess
whether they harbor fewer de novo genes than D. melanogaster. However, at the time of revision (June
2025), we were unable to identify additional AT- or GC-rich insects in NCBI with comparable genome size,
lifestyle, and a sufficient number of sequenced and annotated neighbors. The only potentially “suitable”
species was Apis mellifera (32% GC content). Although A. mellifera has fewer de novo genes than D.
melanogaster (28 vs. 54, respectively), this comparison is not conclusive because A. mellifera has a smaller
genome (9,935 vs. 13,900 genes, respectively) and a drastically different effective population size, as only
the queen transmits genes while most individuals are sterile workers. Robust conclusions would require
clades containing closely related species with contrasting GC contents and enough examples for statistical
power. Therefore, we chose not to elaborate on this case in the manuscript, as this very interesting question
calls for more comprehensive comparative analyses for proper interpretation.
We next investigated biological features that might underlie the discrepancies in the number of de novo
genes across the 22 focal species. Most AT- and GC-rich species are parasitic or opportunistic and, as typical
for parasites, have small genomes with fewer than 10,000 genes. The three exceptions are Rotaria sp., T.
versicolor, and C. reinhardtii, which are free-living organisms with remarkably large gene repertoires despite
low counts of de novo genes. Although our dataset is too small for definitive conclusions, AT-rich species
seem to contain even fewer de novo genes than GC-rich ones. One should note that AT-rich species under
study are more extreme (20-30% GC content) than GC-rich ones, where the most GC-rich species in the
dataset, C. reinhardtii, reaches “only” 64.5% GC content. Furthermore, aggregation is known to be more
detrimental than disorder, which may influence innovation strategies in extreme AT-rich species. Notably,
P. falciparum displays high recombination rates in subtelomeric antigen families, generating antigenic
diversity10–12. E. histolytica shows evidence of bacterial gene acquisitions through horizontal gene
transfer13
and harbors abundant retrotransposons implicated in genome rearrangements14. Finally, Rotaria sp.
exhibits frequent HGTs from non-metazoan sources4. While it remains difficult to draw general conclusions,
these studies raise the hypothesis that these species rely on alternative mechanisms (e.g., recombination,
horizontal gene transfer…) to drive innovation.
We next examined whether a phylogenetic signal exists across the 3,379 species based on their GC content.
New Table S1 shows that GC-rich species mostly consist of Fungi (82%), with the remaining species
belonging to SAR (8%), Chlorophytes (4%), and Discoba (3.5%). In contrast, AT-rich species are more widely

S14). Large genomes (> 1,000 Mbp) are mostly found in intermediate GC-content species, whereas GC-rich
species typically have small genomes (< 100 Mbp). Unlike GC-rich species, AT-rich species feature a broader

Overall, although we observe a relationship between species phylogenetic distribution and GC content, and
extreme GC-content species tend to have fewer de novo candidates, these patterns do not directly match
genome size and lifestyle. Some parasites (e.g., C. javanica, L. infantum) possess many de novo genes,
whereas some large-genome species have few (e.g., Rotaria sp., T. versicolor, C. reinhardtii). Conversely,
small genomes, such as that of S. cerevisiae, still contain many de novo genes, highlighting a complex
relationship between these factors.
These observations, nevertheless, raise exciting questions and provide a basis for future studies to further
explore how species’ lifestyle, phylogeny, and GC content influence de novo gene emergence and whether
GC content limits the ability of some species to evolve through de novo gene birth.

We thank the Reviewer for this very insightful comment, which raises an important point regarding
potential biases introduced by genome annotation protocols, especially in the context of de novo gene
discovery. We fully agree that annotation remains a non-trivial task, particularly for distinguishing between
young coding sequences from noncoding ORFs.
To explore this issue, we focused on Saccharomyces cerevisiae, whose genome is arguably the best
annotated among eukaryotes. To minimize annotation biases arising from heterogeneous annotation
pipelines - an issue we previously discussed in Roginski et al.9 - we prioritized genomes annotated using
standardized approaches, such as those from NCBI or specific genome consortia when possible (e.g.,
Caenorhabditis, Oryza sativa). In the case of S. cerevisiae, we deliberately used the NCBI annotation rather
than the manually curated SGD version to maintain as much consistency as possible with its related species.
For neighboring genomes, we relied on the NCBI S. paradoxus genome, which was available at the start of
the project. For the other Saccharomyces species, we used the published annotations at that time: S.
arboricola from Yue et al. 201715, and S. mikatae, S. kudriavzevii, and S. uvarum from Scannell et al. 201116.
One should note that the manual annotation of S. cerevisiae, available in the Saccharomyces Genome
Database (SGD, version R64-5-1), includes 723 more annotated ORFs than the NCBI version that we used.
However, most of them (683) are labeled "Dubious", meaning, according to SGD, that they are “unlikely to
encode an expressed protein” and, therefore, may not correspond to true protein-coding genes.
Interestingly, in the work of Vakirlis et al.17, 87% of the ORFs classified as Dubious were predicted as
“Emerging” based on the annotation version used in their study (Supplemental Data 1 file from Vakirlis et
al.17). The authors also note that “there is no evidence that emerging ORFs correspond to canonical protein-
coding genes”. In any case, Figure B shows that Dubious ORFs are longer and GC-richer than iORFs in general
(Mann-Whitney U test (one-sided), all P < 1x10-16) and exhibit GC content similar to de novo and canonical
CDSs. While we chose not to consider them for the aforementioned reasons (unlikely to represent actual
protein-coding genes and to maintain consistency with neighboring species’ annotations), their properties
suggest that including them is unlikely to affect our conclusions based on NCBI annotation. Nevertheless,
we cannot exclude the possibility that shorter ORFs with atypical nucleotide composition were also missed
in the SGD annotation.

eukaryotic genome, to assess their potential influence on our conclusions. Our analyses suggest that the

“Investigating newly emerged genes can be affected by annotation, since annotation protocols often rely
on prior knowledge, thereby potentially overlooking ORFs with unusual patterns. To assess this, we focused
on S. cerevisiae, one of the best-annotated genomes, and searched for potential additional coding ORFs that
may have been missed during annotation. We screened yeast iORFs against those of its five neighboring
species, retained those with DIAMONDv281 matches in at least four neighbors, and tested them for
signatures of purifying selection. We identified 23 ORFs under selection, specific to Saccharomyces (Table
S2), and reconstructed their ancestral sequences. Although their GC enrichment was less pronounced than
that of the 227 ancestral ORFs reconstructed based on the S. cerevisiae annotation, these sequences still
differ from iORFs in both GC content and length, remaining longer and GC-richer (Mann-Whitney U test
(one-sided), P = 2.7x10-7 and 2.1x10-2, respectively)(Figure S15). As an additional control, we considered
the study by Wacholder et al.4, who compiled 412 ribosome profiling datasets from S. cerevisiae, producing
the most comprehensive yeast translational landscape to date. Their annotation-independent approach
identified approximately 19,000 translated unannotated ORFs. However, only 14 showed signatures of
selection, nine of which had homologs outside Saccharomyces and were likely ancient4. Among the five
remaining candidates, three were lacking homologs for ancestral reconstruction. Interestingly, the two
reconstructed ancestral sequences are longer (61 and 130 residues) and GC-richer (47% and 42%) than
typical iORFs.
These results suggest that potentially overlooked de novo genes are not numerous and, overall, would not

We thank the Reviewer for raising this point. We have now introduced a new test to identify breakpoints
within a sequence of values for each species – specifically, the medians of the GAN distribution of each
phylostratum. To do so, we fitted three Bayesian piecewise-linear models (null: no breakpoint, one
breakpoint, and two breakpoints) using the mcp package21. Model performance was evaluated by leave-
one-out cross-validation22, extracting the expected log-predictive density (ELPD) and its standard error.
Pairwise ELPD differences were calculated, and a more complex model (e.g., two breakpoints over one
breakpoint, or one breakpoint over null model) was accepted only when its improvement (DELPD) exceeded
the combined standard error. Posterior mean breakpoints were then extracted from the model estimates
and mapped back onto the corresponding phylostrata for the 19 species in which at least one breakpoint
was detected.
This analysis allowed us to pinpoint breakpoints across GAN phylostratigraphies, i.e., the phylostrata
marking the transition to a distinct evolutionary regime. The latest breakpoint generally coincides with the
onset of a plateau in GAN frequencies. In most cases, this occurs at the ancestral ORFs or de novo levels
(8/19) or at the TRG level (7/19), suggesting that GAN frequency plateaus early in evolution. The exceptions
consist of H. sapiens and the two plant species (A. thaliana and O. sativa), where the latest breakpoint
occurs slightly later, at Boreoeutheria, Brassicaceae, and Commelinids, respectively.
Figure 4 and S9 have been updated to display the localization of these breakpoints along the GAN kinetics.

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Roginski et al. examines the impact of GC content on de novo gene birth, an important
topic in gene origination, given that species in different clades may have widely varying GC contents, yet all
likely possess de novo genes in their genomes. The authors identified stop-to-stop intergenic ORFs from
more than 3,000 species, analyzed their hydrophobicity, and used ancestral sequence reconstruction to
study the evolution of ORF hydrophobicity. The topic is both interesting and timely, though it is unclear why
the authors focused solely on HCA scores, given the wide range of ordered and disordered genes in any
given species, and that there is no clear agreement and empirical evidence on whether young de novo
genes are ordered. Below are my comments related to the methods and results.
We would first like to thank the Reviewer for their positive comments and constructive feedback, which we
have fully addressed in our response letter and, where appropriate, in the revised manuscript. Before
addressing the specific comments raised by the Reviewer, we would like to clarify our rationale for using
HCA.
We chose HCA because it is fast and alignment-free, which was crucial for studying millions of fast-evolving
ORFs. Moreover, HCA provides a single score that spans the structural spectrum (from disorder to
aggregation propensities), allowing us to describe the structural properties of a sequence with one unified
metric, rather than relying on multiple tools with distinct outputs (e.g., IUPred23, TANGO24, etc).
aggregation propensities of iORFs with IUPred and TANGO. These results, now presented in Figure S2, are
consistent with the trends predicted by HCA. We observe a positive correlation between disorder
propensity and GC content, and an anticorrelation with aggregation propensity, supporting the hypothesis
that AT-rich genomes contain hydrophobic, aggregation-prone iORFs, while GC-rich ones mostly encode
hydrophilic, disordered iORFs. While these independent tools help corroborate the structural trends
identified with HCA, we remain aware that all of these approaches are computational. However, this

1) While it is understandable that a straightforward approach to identifying ORFs is through STOP-to-STOP
analysis, these are not truly iORFs. I wonder how the results would differ if the authors used a start-to-stop
criterion for ORF identification. Ideally, having start-to-stop data for all species would be the best approach,
but this may not be feasible within the revision timeframe. I suggest that the authors compare STOP-to-
STOP ORFs with start-to-stop ORFs in a subset of species across different clades to provide insights into the
impact of the methodological approach.
We define iORFs from stop-to-stop, not because it is the most straightforward computationally, but
because growing evidence shows that translation frequently initiates at non-AUG codons, making ATG-
based definitions potentially too restrictive. Multiple studies have demonstrated that translation does not
rely exclusively on canonical ATG start codons (e.g., Slavoff et al.26, Cuevas et al.27, Ingolia et al.28, Na et
al.29, Papadopoulos et al.30, Zheng & Zhao31).
For instance, Slavoff et al.26 reported that in H. sapiens, only 43% of small ORF-encoded peptides start with
ATG, 21% with near-cognate codons, and the remaining 36% with other codons (see Figure 2D in Slavoff et
al.). Similarly, in our previous analyses of Ribo-seq data from S. cerevisiae30, we found that only ~50% of
detected translation events initiate at ATGs. Recently, Zheng & Zhao identified 993 peptides from
unannotated ORFs in D. melanogaster via mass spectrometry, of which only 331 began with canonical start
codons31. Notably, those with and without ATG start shared comparable properties in amino acid
composition and genomic context (e.g., intergenic, UTRs, sense, antisense).
Thus, defining iORFs from stop-to-stop ensures we do not systematically exclude many ORFs that could
initiate translation with non-canonical starts. While this definition may add a short N-terminal extension
that in fact would not be translated (if the ORF were to be translated), unlike canonical CDSs - whose
upstream regions differ markedly from their evolved sequence, iORFs are unevolved and their putative
upstream regions (if translated) are not expected to differ significantly in amino acid composition and
patterning from the rest of the sequence.
Nevertheless, to address the Reviewer’s concern, we re-analyzed the dataset used for the original Figure 2
(based on a representative subset of iORFs from the 3,379 genomes), this time defining iORFs from start-
to-stop (with start = ATG). As shown in Figure D, the overall trends remain consistent: iORFs in AT-rich
species tend to display higher HCA scores, while those from intermediate and GC-rich species show
intermediate and lower scores, respectively. Similarly, the frequencies of positively and negatively charged
residues across genomes are in line with our initial findings using the stop-to-stop definition.
While this complementary analysis confirms the robustness of our findings, we chose not to include it in
the main manuscript to maintain focus, and since the manuscript is already quite lengthy. However, we
remain fully open to providing it as supplementary material should the Editors or Reviewers find it helpful.

3) The authors should provide more details on the detection of de novo genes using DENSE. One major
challenge in identifying de novo genes is distinguishing them from rapidly evolving genes. It may be
beneficial to incorporate methods such as HMMER or foldseek to further exclude potential artefacts.
We thank the Reviewer for this insightful comment regarding fast-evolving genes and acknowledge that
our description of the DENSE pipeline lacked sufficient detail. We have expanded the method section to
better introduce the methodology.
DENSE9 is a two-step procedure. It first identifies gene candidates that are taxonomically restricted, by
default at the genus level. To do so, it relies on GenEra32, which screens with DIAMONDv233 the focal
species’ proteome against the nr database. Each CDS is then assigned an evolutionary age, corresponding
to the most distant node in the NCBI phylogeny where DIAMONDv2 has detected the CDS. In cases where
a gene has multiple isoforms, the age of the oldest one is assigned to all isoforms. For each TRG, it then
tests whether the gene was ancestrally noncoding. Therefore, using TBLASTN, DENSE searches for
homology traces in noncoding regions of outgroup species among the neighbors of the focal species. These
species are those (i) lacking the candidate gene and (ii) branching after the last common ancestor node of
the gene family. To validate TBLASTN hits, DENSE uses microsynteny to confirm that the detected
noncoding hits in outgroup species are located at the same locus as the focal de novo gene candidate.
Candidates with at least one syntenic noncoding hit in two or more outgroup species are retained as
potential candidates and then filtered based on remote or structural homology according to the Reviewer’s
suggestion. Indeed, we fully agree that DIAMONDv2 may fail to detect distant homologs that have diverged
beyond recognition. To mitigate this risk, we implemented a filtering strategy to exclude candidates
potentially corresponding to fast-evolving genes:
On the one hand, we screened all de novo CDS candidates against the Pfam database using HMMER34 (e-
value £ 1x10-3), without applying a coverage threshold, in order to remain conservative - that is, we chose
to eliminate any candidate showing a detectable domain match, regardless of the extent of the match, to
reduce the risk of retaining false positives (i.e., fast-evolving genes that may have retained only partial
domain similarity). Any candidate with a significant match outside the genus of the focal species was
removed from the de novo CDS set. For genes with multiple isoforms, all isoforms were screened. If any

(ii) Several computational and experimental studies have investigated this question. Some
reported AT-rich protogenes enriched in transmembrane domains17. Other experimental
studies demonstrated that de novo proteins could fold into partially ordered 3D structures or
be associated with some folding potential25,42–45. These experimental studies are consistent
with other computational analyses, including our own work on yeast, which, although limited
to a small number of species (e.g., S. cerevisiae, D. melanogaster, O. sativa…), showed that de
novo proteins may harbor folding potential, with some even predicted as well-folded46–49.
Motivated by these analyses, we extended the analysis to a larger scale. Notably, because structural
properties are directly influenced by amino acid composition, which itself is shaped by GC content (at least
in unevolved sequences), we analyzed a comprehensive dataset of eukaryotic genomes (all annotated
genomes in NCBI with an assembly level of at least “scaffold” as available on March 6, 2023), encompassing

As explained earlier, we used HCA as our primary metric, since it is fast and alignment-free (which was
critical for large-scale analyses) and provides a single score spanning the structural spectrum from disorder
to aggregation. However, to strengthen our predictions, we have now included two complementary and
independent analyses (TANGO and IUPred), which have corroborated the predictions obtained by HCA.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In their manuscript, “Impact of GC content on de novo gene birth,” Roginski et al. explore the influence of
GC content in non-coding open reading frames on the structure of potentially encoded microproteins.
Notably, as a major merit, their analysis spans an impressive dataset of 3,379 eukaryotic genomes—far
exceeding the scope of previous studies, which have been limited either to specific evolutionary lineages
or to smaller genome sets (e.g., 187 genomes in Basile et al., 2017). For a subset of 22 organisms, they
employ a combination of ancestral sequence reconstruction (ASR)—used here more extensively than in

manuscript’s overall tone.

stability54,80.”). In our study, we use the term folding potential to refer to intrinsic sequence features that
may favor folding or the evolution of a foldable protein, rather than to claim that these iORFs currently
44
adopt stable, well-packed, and well-defined 3D structures. [That said, we fully agree that this needed to be
stated explicitly, and it is now clarified in the revised version - see below.]
Notably, regarding the folding potential, we show that iORFs (depending on GC content) can encode
structural building blocks that resemble those found in folded proteins (see next paragraph and new Figure
S2C). These structural building blocks are identified as HCA clusters. The latter have been shown to
correspond to the elementary structural units of folded proteins62,63. The number, size, and composition of
these clusters, along with the intervening linker regions, are integrated into the HCA score, which serves as
a proxy for predicting an ORF’s folding potential62–64. These structural building blocks may not be sufficient
to drive autonomous folding today, but they could facilitate folding in specific contexts (e.g., upon
interaction with partners, oligomerization, or chaperone assistance25), or evolve toward more stable
structures over time through length extension, refinement of residue composition and patterning, or
domain fusion. In this sense, these iORFs host latent structural potential that may be revealed through
molecular interactions, ORF extension and/or amino acid sequence optimization.
Notably, we have now included a new analysis of HCA cluster sizes in iORFs and CDSs across the 3,379
eukaryotic genomes (new Figure S2C). We find that iORFs in intermediate GC-content species encode HCA
clusters with size distributions comparable to those of CDSs, while extreme AT-rich and GC-rich species
deviate in opposite directions (larger and smaller clusters, respectively)(new Figure S2C). This suggests that
intermediate GC-content species harbor a reservoir of iORFs whose sequence composition and organization
confer a higher propensity to adopt or evolve into what might be described as protofolds.
Overall, our results suggest that such proto-structural features are more common in intermediate GC-
content species, which encode iORFs with a better balance of hydrophobic and hydrophilic residues (Figures
2A and S2C). In contrast, iORFs in GC-rich or AT-rich species often skew toward disorder-prone (high
hydrophilic residue content) or aggregation-prone sequences (high hydrophobic residue content),
respectively.
Furthermore, while we agree that very short proteins are unlikely to fold independently, in intermediate
GC-content species (35-50% GC), the median iORF length is approximately 30-40 amino acids (depending
on GC content), and ancestral iORFs are even longer, with lengths often exceeding 60 residues (Figure S11),
thereby likely further enhancing their folding potential. Overall, our results suggest that iORFs from
intermediate GC-content species share more characteristics with CDSs (e.g., hydrophobic residue content,
elementary structural units of proteins) than iORFs from species with extreme GC content. These findings
support the hypothesis that this reservoir may include microproteins with the capacity to evolve more
stable structures. Indeed, if selected, their folding potential could further increase through ORF extension,
and/or optimization of amino acid composition and patterning via positive selection, as discussed in Aubel
et al.45.
Altogether, our findings suggest that intermediate GC-content species offer a favorable background for the
emergence of structurally competent novel microproteins, with more balanced amino acid compositions
and appropriate structural motifs.
We have revised the Results and Discussion sections to incorporate these new analyses.

L208: What is the cause and what is the consequence in the relationship between DNA and protein
material?
We are not entirely sure we have correctly understood the reviewer’s question. If the question concerns
the direction of causality between DNA and protein constraints - that is, who shaped whom - our study does
not aim to resolve this. Instead, our results indicate that protein foldability imposes a strong constraint on
CDSs in eukaryotic species, regardless of their underlying nucleotide composition.
The phrase “reconciliation between DNA and protein constraints” was not intended to imply a
unidirectional causal relationship, but to emphasize the dual requirements that coding sequences must
satisfy: encoding foldable proteins while being composed of nucleotides that vary in GC content.
Notably, our findings suggest that the need to maintain protein foldability may have influenced the
establishment and structure of the genetic code itself. This suggests a co-evolutionary scenario in which
foldability acted as a key constraint, shaping the correspondence between nucleotide triplets and amino
acids, thereby enabling CDSs to meet both DNA and protein-level constraints.
We have revised the corresponding paragraph to clarify this point:

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The revised manuscript by Roginski et al. has been significantly improved. The scientific rigor, clarity,
and figure quality have all been enhanced. I appreciate that the authors thoughtfully addressed my
comments as well as those of the other reviewers.
One minor point for the abstract: “Depending on GC content, these microproteins exhibit distinct
structural properties, suggesting different cellular impacts of pervasive expression.” This sentence
may need to be revised, as the study does not directly examine pervasive expression, and not all
species exhibit it. A possible alternative could be: “...suggesting different cellular impacts if non-genic

We thank the Reviewer for their positive comments. We acknowledge that our previous formulation
could imply that we investigated translation in the studied genomes, which is not the case. We
therefore edited the sentence following the Reviewer’s suggestion.
“Depending on GC content, these microproteins exhibit distinct structural properties, suggesting
different cellular impacts if non-genic regions are pervasively expressed.”

Overall, we thank the Reviewer for their positive feedback. We address all the points raised below.
Authors: “Genomes can be broadly subdivided into coding and noncoding regions, conceptually
classified as distinct and impermeable entities.”
1
- The term “subdivided” seems unnecessary; “divided” would suffice. The use of “impermeable” is
problematic, since the study addresses the transitions between coding and noncoding regions.
I suggest:
“Genomic regions can be divided into coding and noncoding regions, conceptually considered as
distinct entities.”
This sentence should also be supported with a citation. While this concerns functionality beyond
coding/noncoding annotation, see Graur et al. 2013, GBE regarding as how distinct annotations can
be.
Our intent in this opening sentence was to introduce the historical and conceptual view of genomes
as composed of two distinct domains (coding and noncoding), before highlighting that recent OMICS
studies have revealed the expression of presumed noncoding regions and, ultimately, a transition
across these boundaries.
We revised the sentence for clarity as follows:
“Genomes can be broadly divided into coding and noncoding regions, conceptually considered as
distinct entities.”
Because this opening statement refers to the traditional way genomes are conceptualized rather
than to debates on genomic functionality (e.g., ENCODE), we prefer not to cite Graur et al. (2013),
which focuses on functional interpretations beyond the intent of this sentence and might risk
confusing the reader.

Authors (L31–33): “We show that de novo genes preferentially emerge from GC-rich ORFs with folding
potential, revealing that GC content and foldability, coordinated by the genetic code structure,
together shape the emergence of novel genes.”
- This sentence is redundant. “Coordinated by the genetic code structure” does not add clarity.
I suggest:
“We show that de novo genes preferentially emerge from GC-rich ORFs with folding potential.”
We disagree that the mention of “coordination by the genetic code structure” is redundant and prefer
to retain it as this concept is central to our work. Our results not only show that de novo genes tend to
emerge from GC-rich ORFs with folding potential, but also reveal that the relationship between these
two properties (which stems from the structure of the genetic code) influences the emergence of novel
genes. To clarify this point, we have slightly revised the sentence as follows:
“We show that de novo genes preferentially emerge from GC-rich ORFs with folding potential,
revealing that the interplay between GC content and foldability - rooted in the structure of the genetic
code - shapes the emergence of novel genes.”
